name: Rosa Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Rosa. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a 120-tonne excavator at a big bauxite mine, which is the red rock they make aluminium from. The ore's close to the surface, so we strip off the topsoil, dig the bauxite in long shallow strips and load the trucks, and then the land gets put back and replanted behind us. Twelve-hour days, mostly, and I'm usually the one they put on the tricky bits near the creek line.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's precise. You're digging to a few centimetres, and the GPS screen in the cab shows the design so you can see if you're on grade. What wears me out is the heat in the wet season. On my days off, my brother Paulo and I run a little earthmoving business with one mini excavator, doing house pads and driveways, and I use AI apps every day for the quotes, invoices and the scheduling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the one we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be surprised. I already use it too much for it to be nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped, but the useful bits are still useful. I'd post something about how it runs my invoicing, because a few people at church have asked me how I do it. At work I'd just shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's actually good news. The big mine keeps paying me, and the AI keeps saving me ten hours a month on the side business. Nothing to complain about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at the mine and keep growing the side business on weekends. I'd use the AI to chase more jobs and maybe take on a second small machine in a year or two. I've got about four months saved, and I'd keep it there and put extra into the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty happy, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people at church asked how you do it. What do you tell them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I show them on my phone. I take a photo of a driveway, tell the app the size, and it drafts a quote with my rates in about two minutes. Mrs Okoro from the choir now uses it for her cake orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your brother think of all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paulo does the digging and I do the paperwork and the planning, so he's happy. He says I'm the brains and he's the back. Our dad would have loved it, he always wanted us to have something of our own.

S0.say: I'd say it was overhyped but the useful parts are still useful. I'd post about how it runs my invoicing, since people at church have asked, and just shrug at work.
S0.think: I think it's good news for me, because the mine keeps paying and AI keeps saving me about ten hours a month on my side business. There's nothing to complain about.
S0.do: Keeps working at the mine and grows the weekend earthmoving business with her brother, using AI to find more jobs. Plans a second small machine in a year or two while keeping about four months of savings.
S0.quote: Mrs Okoro from the choir now uses it for her cake orders.
S0.fieldNote: She already uses AI daily for a side business and sees it as practical, not threatening. Her traditional values show in family business pride and her church community. She's the planner of the pair, with her brother doing the digging.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. That one I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for people willing to work and learn, and that's how it's always been. I'd say the mine should train people, not just hand out payouts. I'd say it at work and at church, kindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it suits me. The excavator at the mine will probably get more automated, but the side business is where I'd grow. More automation means cheaper machines and software for small operators like us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put in for the mine's semi-autonomous digging training as soon as it's offered. In the first year, I'd use our savings and a small loan to buy a second mini excavator with GPS guidance, so Paulo can run one and a hired lad the other. I'd keep using AI for quoting and scheduling, and maybe add a booking page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A loan's a risk. Why now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the work's there. We turned away eleven jobs last spring because we only had one machine. If more people are building, someone has to dig the footings, and I'd rather it was us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner say about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis would say make sure the numbers work, which is fair, he's a diesel mechanic and he's careful. He'd look after the machine for us at cost. That's what family does.

S1.say: I'd say it's a chance for people willing to work and learn, as it always has been. I'd say the mine should train people rather than just hand out payouts.
S1.think: I think it suits me, since automation would make machines and software cheaper for small operators like us. The mine job may get more automated, but the side business is where I'd grow.
S1.do: Signs up for the mine's semi-autonomous digging training when offered. Uses savings and a small loan in the first year to buy a second GPS-guided mini excavator, hires a worker and adds an online booking page.
S1.quote: We turned away eleven jobs last spring because we only had one machine.
S1.fieldNote: She sees steady change as an opening for her small business and is willing to take on a loan. Her free-market, family-business values come through clearly. Her partner provides a check on risk and practical help with machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one, AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's a lot faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should get moving rather than wait for the government to fix it. I'd tell my friends to learn the tools and think about what they can do for themselves. But I'd also say it's going to be very hard for a lot of families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it squeezes me from both sides. The mine needs fewer of us, and if robots can dig driveways cheaply, my little business has to compete with that. My advantage is that I'm already using the tools, but that doesn't last long in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on the second machine and keep the savings in cash, maybe push it from four months to six. I'd stay at the mine as long as they'd keep me and offer to help set up the new automated diggers. For the business, I'd pivot to the jobs robots won't be trusted with yet, like digging around old pipes and in tight backyards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Lots of pressure, but I'd still feel like I can steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Paulo the first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we're not buying anything until we've seen what the robots can do. And that he should take every job he can now, while people still want a human. He'd probably sulk about the new machine for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the two-year warning help you, in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps me save and pick my niche. But I'd be lying if I said I knew what the business looks like in 2029. I'd be guessing like everyone else.

S2.say: I'd say people should get moving rather than wait for the government to fix it, and learn the tools. I'd also say it'll be very hard for a lot of families.
S2.think: I think it squeezes me from both sides, since the mine needs fewer of us and robots could undercut my small business. Already using the tools helps, but not for long over two years.
S2.do: Holds off on the second machine and builds cash savings from four towards six months. Stays at the mine and offers to help set up the automated diggers, and shifts the business to tricky jobs robots won't be trusted with yet.
S2.feel: Anxious under pressure, but still feeling able to steer.
S2.quote: He'd probably sulk about the new machine for a week.
S2.fieldNote: Even this confident, adaptive operator feels squeezed by the fast timeline, from the mine and from robot competition. She responds by holding cash and finding a niche rather than retreating. She admitted she can't see what the business looks like by 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now AGI by 2031. The same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like it for planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for anyone who wants to work to find a way. I'd say the mine should help with training, and families and churches should help each other. I'd keep saying people should learn the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years gives me time to set the business up properly. If the robots are coming, I want to be the one owning one, not the one replaced by one. So it's a race, but it's a fair race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the second machine in the first year after all, one that can be upgraded to run on its own later. I'd keep working at the mine for maybe three more years, saving hard. Then I'd go full-time in the business with Paulo, running a couple of semi-automated machines and doing the jobs that still need a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More excited than scared, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said owning one, not being replaced by one. Isn't that expensive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. I'd need a loan from the bank and maybe a bit from Luis's family, who've offered before. But a machine that works while I sleep pays for itself faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to make that happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding we keep talking about would be smaller and later, probably in 2028 instead of next year. And no overseas trip. Luis knows that's the deal.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for anyone who wants to work to find a way. The mine should help with training, and families and churches should help each other.
S3.think: I think five years gives me time to set up the business properly. I'd want to own a robot, not be replaced by one, and it would be a fair race.
S3.do: Buys a second machine in the first year that can be upgraded to run on its own, with a bank loan and possibly help from her partner's family. Keeps working at the mine for about three years, then goes full-time in the business.
S3.feel: Uneasy but more excited than scared.
S3.quote: If the robots are coming, I want to be the one owning one, not the one replaced by one.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns her caution back into ambition, with a clear plan to own automated machines. She'd delay her wedding to fund the business, which shows her priorities. She leans on family money rather than any public support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. I'd like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so people should start learning now and stop arguing about it. I'd tell the young ones at church to learn a trade and the tools that go with it. And I'd say businesses should give their workers a fair chance to move with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think ten years is good for me. I could build the business to three or four machines, some automated, and still have Paulo and maybe a couple of workers. By 2036 I'd want to be the boss, not the operator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the mine within two years to run the business full-time. We'd buy the second machine next year and a third two years later. Luis and I would marry next year as planned and buy a house with a big yard for the machines, and I'd keep using AI for the office side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Proud, even, picturing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Leaving the mine is a big step. What makes you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure, nobody is. But a decade gives me room to fall down and get back up. My dad worked for the same company for twenty-five years and got a handshake at the end. I want something with our name on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guys at the mine who don't want to learn. Some of them are good friends. I'd offer them work if I could, but I can't hire everyone.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so people should start learning now and stop arguing. I'd tell young people at church to learn a trade and its tools, and say businesses should give workers a fair chance to move with them.
S4.think: I think ten years is good for me, with time to build the business to three or four machines, some automated. By 2036 I'd want to be the boss, not the operator.
S4.do: Leaves the mine within two years to run the business full-time, buying a second machine next year and a third two years later. Marries her partner next year as planned and buys a house with a large yard for the machines.
S4.quote: My dad worked for the same company for twenty-five years and got a handshake at the end.
S4.fieldNote: The long timeline lets her fully commit to ownership and family plans together. Her father's experience is a strong motive for building something of her own. She worries about friends who won't adapt but is realistic about how many she could hire.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. What would help is cheaper small business loans and less paperwork for people starting out, plus short training courses at the mine for the new systems. I don't want a payment, I want a fair shot.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about women in mining. When I started, people thought I wouldn't last. Now I'm the one running a business on the side. If the robots come, I'd like the women to be owning some of them too.

headlineQuote: I want something with our name on it.
portrait: Rosa is a 27-year-old excavator operator at a large bauxite mine who runs a weekend earthmoving business with her brother Paulo, using AI apps every day for quotes and scheduling. She has about four months saved, a partner, Luis, who's a diesel mechanic, and strong ties to her church and family. She's calm in the plateau and steady change, seeing a chance to grow the business. AGI in two years makes her anxious and pushes her to hold cash and find a niche, while five and ten years let her invest in automated machines and plan to leave the mine and be the boss.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would squeeze both her mine job and her small business at once.
whatWouldHelp: Cheaper small business loans, less paperwork for people starting out, and short training courses at the mine for the new systems.
